overview: Alioramus remotus and the later-described A. altai were small tyrannosaurs from the Late Cretaceous Nemegt Formation of Mongolia, notable for their elongated, low skulls bearing a row of small hornlets along the nasal bones — unlike the deep skull of Tarbosaurus, which shared the same ecosystem. This has led to debate about whether Alioramus represents a distinct lineage or a juvenile Tarbosaurus.

Phylogenetic analyses consistently place Alioramus within Tyrannosauridae, closer to Asian tyrannosaurs than to Tyrannosaurus. The gracile skull and relatively slender build compared to Tarbosaurus suggest that if these two were adults of the same species, we would expect more intermediate forms — the balance of evidence favours Alioramus as a genuine distinct taxon.

fossilSites.name: Nemegt Formation
fossilSites.note: Late Cretaceous fluvial and aeolian deposits sharing Tarbosaurus, ankylosaurs, hadrosaurs and sauropods with Alioramus.

articles.title: Discovery and debate
articles.body: Alioramus remotus was described by Kurzanov in 1976 from a skull and foot material. A more complete species, A. altai, was described in 2009 by Novas and colleagues from a nearly complete juvenile-like skeleton. The juvenility hypothesis — that Alioramus is a young Tarbosaurus — is rejected on the basis of bone texture indicating skeletal maturity and consistent morphological differences from Tarbosaurus at comparable sizes.

articles.title: Skull morphology
articles.body: The nasal hornlets distinguish Alioramus from all other known tyrannosaurids. The skull is proportionally low and long compared to the deep robust skull of Tarbosaurus. The teeth are slightly more numerous than in Tarbosaurus for the jaw length. These differences are consistent with dietary niche partitioning within the Nemegt ecosystem.

articles.title: Ecology
articles.body: Two tyrannosaurs in the same formation — Tarbosaurus (large, robust) and Alioramus (smaller, gracile) — likely partitioned prey resources differently, analogous to how lions and cheetahs exploit different prey sizes in modern African ecosystems. Alioramus probably took smaller prey than the apex predator Tarbosaurus.

fossilRecord.material: Skull and partial skeletal material; best known from Late Cretaceous Mongolian specimens.
fossilRecord.paleo: Nemegt floodplain deposits preserve large tyrannosaurids, ornithomimosaurs, oviraptorosaurs and hadrosaurs.
fossilRecord.evidence: Long, low skull and many small teeth distinguish it from deeper-skulled tyrannosaurids.

record.description: Alioramus was a long-snouted tyrannosaurid from the Maastrichtian Nemegt Formation of Mongolia. A. remotus is based on a fragmentary skull and foot bones, while the better-preserved A. altai provides most detailed anatomical information.
facts: A. altai preserves a substantially complete skull and partial skeleton of a subadult.
The distinctive row of low nasal rugosities is real; their display role is an inference.

review.ageReviewNote: Both named species come from the Maastrichtian Nemegt Formation.
